kurals.tamil:
வாளற்றுப் புற்கென்ற கண்ணும் அவர்சென்ற
நாளொற்றித் தேய்ந்த விரல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaalatrup purkendra kannum avarsendra
naalotrith thaeyndha viral.
kurals.meaning: My eyes have lost their brightness and grown dim from watching the road for him, and my fingers are worn from touching the marks I made for each day since he left.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone you love goes on a long trip. Every day you stand at the window looking down the road, and every night you make a mark on the wall and count them all again. After many days your eyes are tired from looking and your finger is sore from counting. That is how much the lady in this verse misses her husband.
kurals.university: Chapter 127, avarvayiṉ vitumpal (‘eager longing for him’; vitumpal = impatient yearning), continues the kaṟpu (wedded love) section: the time the husband (talaivaṉ) fixed for his return is passing, and the wife (talaivi) speaks her impatience; in two couplets (1268, 1270) the husband’s own eagerness is voiced, which is why Pope titles the chapter ‘Mutual Desire’. Here the heroine offers two physical proofs: her eyes are vāḷ aṟṟu (stripped of their lustre, vāḷ = brightness) and puṟkeṉṟa (dimmed, unable to see fine things, as Solomon Pappaiah glosses), and her finger is worn from nāḷ oṟṟi, pressing the day-marks she has drawn on the wall; Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all supply the wall (சுவர்) on which the days are scored. The commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as the heroine telling her friend (tōḻi) that she can no longer bear the delay. The couplet reads identically on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa’s Cloud Messenger, the exiled yaksha pictures his wife at home counting the months still left of their separation by laying flowers on the threshold, one for each, and wasting with longing.
hinduism.explanation: Classical Sanskrit love poetry gives the separated wife a counting ritual very like the Kural’s day-marks on the wall.
hinduism.tie_back: Both wives keep a tally of the days apart, and both are worn down by the counting itself.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Meghaduta (Uttaramegha), the yaksha’s description of his wife (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a very close parallel (counting the days of separation), though from classical court poetry rather than scripture, and verse numbering varies by edition so none is given.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am weary of my crying: my throat is dried: mine eyes fail while I wait for my God.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes waiting so long and so hard that his eyes give out.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same of her eyes: they have lost their light from watching for the one she waits for.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a close image of eyes failing from waiting, though the psalmist waits for God, not a spouse.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s long grief for his absent son Joseph costs him his sight.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, years of longing for an absent loved one are written in the eyes, which lose their brightness.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a strong match on eyes dimmed by longing, though the bond is a father’s for his son rather than a wife’s for her husband.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Mine eyes fail for Thy word, saying: ‘When wilt Thou comfort me?’”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist’s eyes wear out as he keeps asking when the promised comfort will come.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s dimmed eyes carry the same unspoken question: when will he come back?
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); same image of eyes failing in waiting, applied to God’s promise rather than a returning husband.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names not seeing the one you love as one of the basic forms of suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s worn eyes and fingers are exactly the pain of not seeing the beloved, though the Buddha’s answer is to loosen the attachment rather than keep counting.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it names the same pain, but its counsel (avoid such attachment) runs against the Kural’s celebration of devoted longing.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the daughter of the king heard of the ordination of the Gina, laughter and gaiety forsook her, and she was overwhelmed with affliction.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati, betrothed to Arishtanemi, is left grieving when he turns away from their wedding to become a monk.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati’s lost gaiety is the Jain counterpart of the heroine’s lost brightness of eye: both are women worn down by a beloved’s absence.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a genuine Jain picture of a woman’s grief at separation, but Arishtanemi will not return, and the story goes on to praise Rajimati’s own renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Penelope weeps for Odysseus as she listens to the disguised stranger, her cheeks melting with tears like snow thawing on the mountains, though her husband sits beside her unrecognised.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s faithful wife has spent nearly twenty years waiting, and her grief shows in her face.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope’s tear-worn face and the heroine’s dimmed eyes are the same mark of long waiting for a husband.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous simile; a good parallel on a wife marked by long waiting, though Homer has no counting of days.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Roland Barthes, describing the lover’s experience of waiting, suggests that the lover is defined as the one who waits, and that waiting itself is a kind of enchantment that fixes the lover in place.
philosophy.explanation: Barthes treats waiting not as empty time but as the very shape that love takes in absence.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s whole existence has become waiting: eyes on the road, finger on the calendar.
philosophy.source: Roland Barthes, A Lover’s Discourse: Fragments, ‘Waiting’ (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a modern essay figure; a good conceptual match on waiting as love’s form, but it is literary theory rather than a classical ethical source.

kurals.tamil:
இலங்கிழாய் இன்று மறப்பின்என் தோள்மேல்
கலங்கழியும் காரிகை நீத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Ilangizhaai indru marappin-en thoalmael
kalangazhiyum kaarikai neeththu.
kurals.meaning: Friend in shining jewels, if I were to forget him even now, my arms would lose their beauty and the bangles would slip from them.
kurals.elementary: A girl tells her best friend: “Even though missing him hurts, I won’t stop thinking about him. If I tried to forget him, I would only become sadder and thinner, so thin that my bracelets would fall off.” Remembering him, even when it is hard, is what keeps her going.
kurals.university: The heroine addresses her friend as ilaṅkiḻāy, ‘you of shining ornaments’ (Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take the addressee as the tōḻi; Solomon Pappaiah’s gloss ஒளிரும் நகை அணிந்தவனே uses a masculine ending, apparently a slip). Kalam aḻiyum (‘the ornaments come off’) is the stock Tamil sign of a wasting body: the arms (tōḷ) grow thin and the bangles slide off, and kārikai (beauty, grace) departs. The logic is a reversal: one might expect forgetting to ease her pain, but she says that even to try to forget him today would ruin her further, so she chooses to keep remembering. The Drew/Lazarus explanation printed on ytamizh.com reads ‘even in the other life’, reflecting a reading of iṉṟu that some commentators extend; the main modern glosses take iṉṟu simply as ‘today, while I suffer’. The Tamil text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ashoka grove, Hanuman finds Sita pale and thin, wearing a single braid and no ornaments, her thoughts fixed on Rama alone.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki pictures the separated Sita as a wife whose body is wasting while her mind never leaves her husband.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita and the Kural’s heroine both lose their outward beauty in separation yet refuse to let the beloved slip from memory.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known description; strong match on beauty fading while memory of the husband holds firm, though Sita is captive rather than left at home.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.”
christianity.explanation: God answers the fear of being forgotten with a promise stronger than a mother’s memory.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine makes the same vow toward her husband: whatever it costs her, she will not forget him.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); shares the refusal to forget, but the speaker is God and the bond is parental, not marital.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi opens the Masnavi with the reed flute, cut from its reed-bed, whose every note is a lament of separation and a longing to return to the source it remembers.
islam.explanation: For Rumi the soul’s song comes from remembering where it belongs; the remembering is both its pain and its life.
islam.tie_back: Like the reed, the heroine keeps the absent one alive in memory, and that remembering is what sustains her.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi I.1-18, ‘Song of the Reed’ (tr. R.A. Nicholson; paraphrase)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; a good fit on memory of the beloved as the substance of longing, though Rumi’s beloved is ultimately divine.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning. Let my tongue cleave to the roof of my mouth, if I remember thee not; if I set not Jerusalem above my chiefest joy.”
judaism.explanation: The exiles in Babylon bind their own bodies to their memory of Zion.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural uses the very same structure: if I forget, let my body suffer for it, with arms that lose their beauty and bangles that fall.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a striking structural match (an oath that the body will fail if memory fails), though the object is a city, not a spouse.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Nakula’s father and Nakula’s mother tell the Buddha that they have never been unfaithful even in thought and wish to see each other in this life and in lives to come; the Buddha says that a couple matched in faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom will meet again.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha treats a devoted couple’s wish to remain together as something that shared virtue can sustain.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s refusal to forget her husband is the same steadfast devotion that the Buddha praises in this model couple.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 4.55, Samajivina Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu; paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sutta; a good match on unwavering marital devotion, though it does not deal with separation or its physical toll.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Firm and decided she cut off her tresses which were black like bees and dressed with a brush and comb.”
jainism.explanation: Abandoned by Arishtanemi, Rajimati gives up her beauty deliberately and becomes a nun.
jainism.tie_back: Both women lose their adornment in separation, but Rajimati lays it down by choice to follow the path, while the Kural’s heroine fears losing it and clings to memory instead.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a contrast rather than a parallel: Jain scripture turns lost beauty into renunciation, the opposite of the Kural’s devoted remembering.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s letter of Laodamia to Protesilaus at Troy, she says she has no care to comb her hair or wear gold-woven clothes while her husband is at war, and that she lives on thoughts of him.
greek_mythology.explanation: The mythic wife lets her beauty go untended because her whole mind is with the absent husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Laodamia and the Kural’s heroine both let outward grace fall away while holding their husband constantly in mind.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Ovid’s retelling of a Greek myth; a close parallel on neglected beauty and constant remembrance, though Ovid is a Latin poet.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that distance does not break friendship outright but interrupts its activity, and that a long absence seems to make people forget it, citing the saying that lack of converse has broken many a friendship.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle sees forgetting as the natural danger of long absence.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine sees the same danger and refuses it: she will not let absence turn into forgetting.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 8.5 (tr. W.D. Ross; paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; good fit on absence leading to forgetting, though Aristotle is analysing friendship, not married love.

kurals.tamil:
உரன்நசைஇ உள்ளம் துணையாகச் சென்றார்
வரல்நசைஇ இன்னும் உளேன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Urannasaii ullam thunaiyaakach chendraar
varalnasaii innum ulen.
kurals.meaning: He went away seeking victory, with only his own resolve for company; I am still alive only because I long to see him come back.
kurals.elementary: A brave soldier leaves home to win a great contest, taking only his courage with him. His wife at home is very sad, but one thing keeps her going: the hope of seeing him walk back through the door. That hope is like a lamp that keeps her heart from going dark.
kurals.university: The couplet balances two desires with the same verb, nacai (‘longing’, here in the old verbal form nacaii): he left out of uraṉ nacai, desire for strength or victory, with uḷḷam tuṇaiyāka, his own spirit as his only companion; she lives on out of varal nacai, desire for his return. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss uraṉ as victory (வெற்றி) and uḷḷam as zeal (ஊக்கம்); Solomon Pappaiah adds a note of reproach, reading that he spurned her companionship to make his resolve his companion. Iṉṉum uḷēṉ, ‘I still exist’, implies that only this hope keeps her alive, a recurring motif in the kaṟpu section. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sita tells Hanuman that she will keep herself alive for one more month in the hope that Rama will come for her, and that she cannot live beyond that.
hinduism.explanation: Sita’s life in captivity is sustained only by the expectation of her husband’s coming.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Sita says plainly that she lives on only for the day of his return.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda, Sita’s message to Rama through Hanuman (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; very close in sense (life held only for the beloved’s coming), though the sarga number is not given because editions differ.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes hope as the patient waiting for what is not yet seen.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine lives in exactly that hope: she cannot see him, but waiting for him keeps her alive.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); fits the structure of sustaining hope, but Paul speaks of cosmic redemption, not a spouse’s return.

islam.quote_or_event: “[Jacob] said, ‘Rather, your souls have enticed you to something, so patience is most fitting. Perhaps Allah will bring them to me all together. Indeed it is He who is the Knowing, the Wise.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob, having lost two sons, holds on through patience and the hope that they will be returned to him.
islam.tie_back: The heroine’s will to live rests on the same hope that the absent one will be brought back.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a solid match on hope of return sustaining the one left behind, though the bond is parental.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Israel said: ‘It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive; I will go and see him before I die.’”
judaism.explanation: Jacob’s spirit revives at the news that Joseph lives, and seeing him becomes the one thing left to live for.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine too is kept alive by one wish: to see him again.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); close in feeling (life oriented toward seeing the absent one), though parental rather than marital.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Sambula Jataka, the princess Sambula follows her husband into the forest when he falls gravely ill and tends him faithfully, refusing to abandon him.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka holds up Sambula as a model of a wife whose devotion carries her through hardship.
buddhism.tie_back: Sambula’s steadfastness and the heroine’s will to live for her husband’s return are the same devotion under strain.
buddhism.source: Sambula Jataka (Jataka No. 519, tr. E.B. Cowell et al.; paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a Jataka story; it shares wifely devotion through hardship, but it is about caring for a sick husband, not waiting for an absent one.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jacobi notes that Rajimati’s lament for Arishtanemi became the subject of a Jain Sanskrit poem, the Nemidutakavya of Vikrama, in which each stanza ends with a line borrowed from Kalidasa’s Meghaduta, turning her into a separated lover sending a message to her beloved.
jainism.explanation: Jain poets themselves took up the viraha (separation) form to voice Rajimati’s longing for the Jina.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Rajimati in this poem lives in longing for one who has gone away on a lofty purpose of his own.
jainism.source: Nemidutakavya of Vikrama, as described in Hermann Jacobi’s note to Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.28 (SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: The existence and form of the poem were verified in Jacobi’s note on sacred-texts.com, but its text was not consulted; a later poem, not canonical scripture, and the beloved here never returns.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: While Ceyx is at sea, his wife Alcyone burns incense to the gods every day, weaves garments for his homecoming and prays for his safe return, not knowing he has already drowned.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s myth shows a wife whose every day is organised around her husband’s expected return.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Alcyone and the Kural’s heroine both live for the moment the absent husband comes home.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Ovid’s retelling of a Greek myth; good match on living for a husband’s return, though the story ends in tragedy and transformation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Nietzsche writes that if we have our own why of life, we can put up with almost any how.
philosophy.explanation: A clear reason to live makes even hard conditions bearable.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s ‘why’ is his return, and it is what lets her endure the ‘how’ of separation.
philosophy.source: Friedrich Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols, ‘Maxims and Arrows’ 12 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known maxim; a good structural fit, though Nietzsche is speaking generally, not of love.

kurals.tamil:
கூடிய காமம் பிரிந்தார் வரவுள்ளிக்
கோடுகொ டேறுமென் நெஞ்சு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kootiya kaamam pirindhaar varavullik
koaduko daerumen nenju.
kurals.meaning: Thinking of the return of the one who left the love we shared, my heart climbs from branch to branch to look out for him.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever climbed a tree to see far away? The lady in this verse feels so excited thinking her husband might be coming home that it is as if her heart climbs up into the treetops, branch after branch, trying to spot him on the road.
kurals.university: The striking image is kōṭu koṭu ēṟum eṉ neñcu, ‘my heart climbs branch upon branch’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take it literally as the heart climbing to the treetop to watch the road; Sivayogi Sivakumar compares it to a creeper that outgrows the pole it climbs; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as the heart, freed of sorrow, spreading branches and growing upward in joy, which is close to Pope’s ‘my heart with rapture swells’. Kūṭiya kāmam pirintār, ‘he who parted from the love we had joined in’, recalls their earlier union. The commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar takes the couplet as the heroine’s eager anticipation at news or thought of his coming. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, Radha’s companion describes her waiting for Krishna in the forest bower, starting at every rustle and decking the bower in expectation of his coming.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s Radha lives in a state of eager, restless anticipation of her beloved’s arrival.
hinduism.tie_back: Radha’s restless watching is the same leap of the heart the Kural pictures as climbing branch after branch.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Radha’s waiting in the bower (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a recurring scene; a good emotional match, though canto numbers are not given and Radha’s situation is a tryst, not a husband’s return.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Hope deferred maketh the heart sick: but when the desire cometh, it is a tree of life.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb sets the sickness of delayed hope against the life that floods back when the desire is fulfilled.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine’s heart, at the very thought of his return, rises like a tree; the proverb uses the same image for fulfilled desire.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong match on delayed hope and its fulfilment, with a shared tree image, though the proverb is general.

islam.quote_or_event: As the caravan carrying Joseph’s shirt leaves Egypt, Jacob tells those around him that he perceives the scent of Joseph, even though they think him weak in mind.
islam.explanation: Before any news arrives, the longing father’s heart already senses that his son is on the way back to him.
islam.tie_back: The heroine’s heart likewise runs ahead to meet the returning beloved before he has arrived.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the verse’s wording was not re-verified this session; a good match on the heart anticipating a loved one’s return, though the bond is parental.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hark! my beloved! behold, he cometh, leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills. My beloved is like a gazelle or a young hart; behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh in through the windows, he peereth through the lattice.”
judaism.explanation: The bride hears and imagines her beloved’s approach before he has even reached her.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s heart climbing to look out for him is the same eager picture of a lover’s coming.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a close match on eager anticipation of the beloved’s approach, though the Song’s lovers are not separated spouses.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The craving of one given to heedless living grows like a creeper. Like the monkey seeking fruits in the forest, he leaps from life to life (tasting the fruit of his kamma).”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures craving as a creeper and a monkey, always climbing and leaping toward the next thing it wants.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart climbing branch to branch is almost the same image, though the Kural celebrates the climbing while the Dhammapada warns against it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a close image (creeper and branch-leaping monkey), but the moral judgment is reversed.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Cast aside from you all attachments, as the (leaves of) a lotus let drop off the autumnal water, exempt from every attachment, Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira tells Gautama to let attachments fall away as water runs off a lotus leaf.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heart reaches up and out toward the beloved; Jain teaching counsels the opposite movement, letting attachment drop away.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; included as a candid contrast, since Jain scripture offers no praise of eager longing for a spouse.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Night after night, Hero climbs her tower at Sestos and lights a lamp, watching across the Hellespont for Leander to swim to her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hero’s tower and lamp make her whole being a watch for the beloved’s coming.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hero climbs her tower to watch for him; the Kural’s heroine sends her heart up the branches to do the same.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the late Greek poem; a strong image match on climbing to watch for the beloved, though the story ends in tragedy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines hope as an inconstant pleasure arising from the idea of something future or past whose outcome we still doubt.
philosophy.explanation: Hope, for Spinoza, is a real joy, but an unsteady one, because it depends on something not yet certain.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s heart leaps with exactly this inconstant joy at the mere thought of his return.
philosophy.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics III, Definitions of the Affects 12 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a standard definition; good conceptual fit for anticipatory joy, though Spinoza is analysing emotions, not describing love.

kurals.tamil:
காண்கமன் கொண்கனைக் கண்ணாரக் கண்டபின்
நீங்கும்என் மென்தோள் பசப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaankaman konkanaik kannaarak kandapin
neengum-en men-dhoal pasappu.
kurals.meaning: Let me only see my husband until my eyes are full; once I have seen him, the pallor on my slender arms will fade away by itself.
kurals.elementary: When you are missing someone, you can feel pale and tired. But the moment you see them, you feel better right away. The lady in this verse says: “I just need to see him properly, and all my paleness will disappear like magic.”
kurals.university: Kāṇka maṉ is an optative: ‘may I see’, with maṉ marking an intense wish. Koṇkaṉ, ‘husband’ (originally ‘lord of the seashore’ in the neytal landscape), is to be seen kaṇṇāra, ‘to the eyes’ full’. Pacappu is pacalai, the sallow pallor that in Tamil love convention spreads over a woman’s body in separation; chapter 119 is devoted to it. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar say it will vanish ‘of itself’ (தானே) once she sees him, so the cure is sight alone. The commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar treats this as her answer to the friend who urges patience. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna reappears among the gopis after vanishing from the rasa dance, they rise up all at once, their eyes wide with love, as if life had returned to their bodies.
hinduism.explanation: In the Bhagavata, the mere sight of the returning beloved revives those who were wasting in separation.
hinduism.tie_back: The heroine expects exactly this: one full look at him and her pallor will vanish.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.32.2-3 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada; paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not re-verified this session; very close on sight of the beloved restoring life, within a devotional frame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And ye now therefore have sorrow: but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus promises his grieving disciples that seeing him again will turn their sorrow into lasting joy.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same promise to herself: seeing him will cure her sorrow.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); close on reunion-by-sight healing grief, though the relationship is master and disciples.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when the bearer of good tidings arrived, he cast it over his face, and he returned [once again] seeing. He said, ‘Did I not tell you that I know from Allah that which you do not know?’”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s sight, lost through grief for Joseph, returns when Joseph’s shirt is laid on his face.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, the bodily mark of separation is healed by contact with the beloved’s return.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a striking match on a separation-illness cured by reunion, though parental rather than marital.

judaism.quote_or_event: “O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the covert of the cliff, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet is thy voice, and thy countenance is comely.”
judaism.explanation: The lover asks only to see the beloved’s face and hear her voice.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s whole wish is the same: let me see him, and that will be enough.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); close on longing simply to see the beloved, without the Kural’s image of pallor cured.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The introduction to the Canda-Kinnara Jataka tells how, when the Buddha first returned to Kapilavatthu, Yasodhara stayed in her chamber, saying he would come to her if she had any worth; he came, and she held his feet and wept.
buddhism.explanation: The commentarial story gives Yasodhara a long, faithful waiting rewarded by the sight of her former husband.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Yasodhara’s long sorrow finds release the moment she sees him again.
buddhism.source: Canda-Kinnara Jataka (Jataka No. 485), introductory story (tr. E.B. Cowell et al.; paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of commentarial narrative, not canonical sutta; partial fit, since the Buddha returns as a renunciant and the reunion leads to her own ordination later.

jainism.quote_or_event: “After practising severe austerities both of them became Kêvalins, and having completely annihilated their Karman, they reached the highest perfection.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati and Rathanemi end not in reunion with a beloved but in liberation, each through their own discipline.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine expects healing from seeing her husband; the Jain story places final healing in liberation rather than in any human reunion.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a contrast, not a parallel: Jainism locates the end of suffering in liberation, not in the sight of a beloved.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles brings a veiled woman back from the dead to Admetus, who at first refuses her; when the veil is lifted he sees his wife Alcestis and his grief turns to joy.
greek_mythology.explanation: Euripides stages a reunion in which the mere sight of the lost wife ends the mourning.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Admetus’ grief, like the heroine’s pallor, vanishes the moment he sees the one he lost.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene; partial fit, since the separation was death rather than a journey and the roles of husband and wife are reversed.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Phaedrus, Socrates says that when the soul is parted from the beloved it is stung and in pain, but when it looks on the beloved again it is refreshed and its pangs cease.
philosophy.explanation: Plato describes the lover’s suffering in absence and the relief that comes from sight of the beloved.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point in philosophical form: separation makes the lover ill, and seeing the beloved heals.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage; a very close match on pain in absence relieved by sight, though Plato’s account serves his theory of the soul.

kurals.tamil:
வருகமன் கொண்கன் ஒருநாள் பருகுவன்
பைதல்நோய் எல்லாம் கெட.
kurals.transliteration:
Varukaman kon-kan oru-naal parukuvan
paidhalnhoi ellaam keda.
kurals.meaning: Let my husband come back just one day, and I will drink in his presence until all this grieving sickness is gone.
kurals.elementary: When you are very thirsty, a cool drink makes you feel better all over. The lady says being with her husband again would be like that: after missing him for so long, being with him would wash away all her sadness.
kurals.university: Again an optative: varuka maṉ, ‘may he come’, with oru nāḷ, ‘even one day’, suggesting that a single day would suffice. Parukuvaṉ, ‘I shall drink’, is the chapter’s boldest metaphor: she will take in his presence as one drinks to slake thirst (Pope: ‘I’ll drink that nectar’), so that paital nōy, the anguished sickness of separation, is wholly destroyed (ellām keṭa). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss parukuvaṉ as ‘enjoy fully’ (நுகர்வேன்), and Puliyur Kesikan as ‘drink in delight’ (இன்பத்தை பருகுவேன்). The image belongs to the conventions of akam poetry and should be read as the delight of reunion. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the gopis meet Krishna again at Kurukshetra after long separation, they drink him in with their eyes, cursing the creator of eyelids for interrupting their gaze, and embrace him within their hearts.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata pictures reunion as a thirsty drinking-in of the beloved through the eyes.
hinduism.tie_back: The gopis and the Kural’s heroine use the same metaphor: the long-absent beloved is drunk in until the pain of separation is gone.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.82 (Krishna meets the gopis at Kurukshetra) (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not re-verified this session; a close match on drinking in the beloved after separation, within a devotional frame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It was but a little that I passed from them, but I found him whom my soul loveth: I held him, and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother’s house, and into the chamber of her that conceived me.”
christianity.explanation: After searching the city at night, the bride finds her beloved and holds him fast.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine longs for exactly this: to have him back and not let go until all the ache of absence is gone.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); a strong match on the joy of recovering the absent beloved.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of His signs is that He created for you from yourselves mates that you may find tranquillity in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an names a spouse as a source of tranquillity, bound by affection and mercy.
islam.tie_back: The heroine seeks just that: in her husband’s return she will find rest from her anguish.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); a fitting general statement on spouses as peace for one another, without the Kural’s separation context.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Stay ye me with dainties, refresh me with apples; for I am love-sick.”
judaism.explanation: The bride calls herself love-sick and asks to be revived with sweet things.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also names her longing a sickness and expects to drink her cure in the beloved’s presence.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); close on love-sickness and its sweet remedy, though the Song does not frame it as separation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Canda-Kinnara Jataka, a king shoots the kinnara Canda; his wife Canda laments over him until Sakka restores him to life, and the two rejoice together again.
buddhism.explanation: The Jataka tells of a wife’s grief over her lost husband turned to joy when he is restored to her.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, the kinnari’s sorrow ends only with her husband given back to her.
buddhism.source: Canda-Kinnara Jataka (Jataka No. 485, tr. E.B. Cowell et al.; paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a Jataka love story; good match on reunion ending a wife’s grief, though the separation is caused by violence, not a journey.

jainism.quote_or_event: Citta and Sambhuta, brothers through five successive births, are born apart in the sixth; when they meet again, Citta the monk urges King Brahmadatta to renounce, but Brahmadatta, bound by pleasures, cannot.
jainism.explanation: The Jain story of a long-separated pair reunited turns the reunion into a test of whether one can let go of worldly delight.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine longs to drink in the delight of reunion; the Jain reunion story warns that such delight is what binds the soul.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13, Citta and Sambhuta (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45; paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a canonical story not re-read this session; a reunion after separation, but between brothers and with the opposite moral.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Penelope at last recognises Odysseus, Homer compares her joy to that of shipwrecked sailors who reach the shore, and she cannot take her arms from around his neck.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Odyssey’s great reunion turns twenty years of grief into overwhelming relief.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the reunion the Kural’s heroine longs for, when all her anguish will drain away at once.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous simile; a strong match on reunion washing away long grief.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Symposium, Aristophanes says that love is the desire and pursuit of the whole, the healer who seeks to make one of two and so cure the wound of human nature.
philosophy.explanation: Aristophanes’ myth treats love as the cure for the pain of having been divided from one’s other half.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine likewise sees reunion with her husband as the cure for the sickness of separation.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known speech; good match on love as healing separation, though Aristophanes’ myth is comic and universal.

kurals.tamil:
புலப்பேன்கொல் புல்லுவேன் கொல்லோ கலப்பேன்கொல்
கண்அன்ன கேளிர் விரன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pulappaen-kol pulluvaen kolloa kalappaenkol
kan-anna kaelir viran.
kurals.meaning: When he comes back, he who is as dear to me as my own eyes, shall I sulk at him, or embrace him, or do both together? I cannot decide.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your best friend went away for a long time without visiting. When they finally come back, part of you wants to say “Hmph, where were you?” and part of you wants to give them a big hug. The lady in this verse feels both at once, and she just can’t decide which to do first.
kurals.university: Three rhetorical questions, each with the doubt particle kol: pulappēṉ (shall I show pulavi, the lover’s feigned sulk), pulluvēṉ (shall I embrace), kalappēṉ (shall I mingle the two, or simply unite). Kaṇ aṉṉa kēḷir, ‘the beloved who is like my eyes’, and viraṉ (‘should he come’) set the scene. Solomon Pappaiah reads kalappēṉ as ‘doing both together’ and Kalaignar adds that she is too overwhelmed even to know; the couplet anticipates the later chapters on ūṭal (lovers’ quarrel, chapters 131-133). Textual note: ytamizh.com’s ‘English Couplet’ slot for 1267 contains a prose explanation, and its ‘Couplet Explanation’ (‘This malady (of lust) is manured by the talk of women…’) belongs to Kural 1147, not this couplet. The Tamil text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, when Krishna comes to Radha at dawn after a night away, she rebukes him in wounded pride, and only later, after his pleading, does her anger melt into reconciliation.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva gives Radha the full sequence of māna (proud sulk) followed by reunion.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees both moves ahead of her, the sulk and the embrace, and cannot choose between them.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, Radha’s rebuke and reconciliation (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s central arc; strong match on pique and reconciliation, though Radha’s anger has a specific cause and canto numbers are not given.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, saying, Open to me… I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?”
christianity.explanation: The bride’s heart wakes for her beloved, yet she hesitates and makes excuses before rising.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she is caught between eager love and a reluctance that holds her back.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV; ellipsis marks an omitted phrase); good fit on ambivalence at the beloved’s coming, though her hesitation is not a sulk.

islam.quote_or_event: “I know when you are pleased with me or angry with me… When you are pleased with me, you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Muhammad,’ but when you are angry with me, then you say, ‘No, by the Lord of Abraham.’” Aisha replies that even then she leaves nothing but his name.
islam.explanation: The Prophet gently notices Aisha’s small sulks, and she answers that even in anger her love for him remains.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s mix of pulavi and embrace: the sulk is only on the surface, and the love beneath it never leaves.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com (ellipsis marks an omitted line; Aisha’s reply paraphrased); a close match on loving pique between spouses.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him; and they wept.”
judaism.explanation: After twenty years of estrangement and grievance, Esau meets Jacob not with reproach but with an embrace.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wonders whether her grievance or her embrace will win; in Esau’s case the embrace wins.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); next-best match: resentment giving way to embrace at reunion, but between brothers, not lovers.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From affection springs grief, from affection springs fear. For one who is wholly free from affection there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces both grief and fear to the root of affection.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s sulk and her embrace both spring from one root, her love, which is just what the verse names as the source of turmoil.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; next-best match: it explains the root of her mixed feelings but counsels freedom from them rather than celebrating them.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having heard the Buddha’s well-delivered sermon, adorned by illustrations, Gautama cut off love and hatred and reached perfection.”
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching names love (raga) and hatred (dvesha) as the twin bonds to be cut for liberation (‘Buddha’ here is a title for Mahavira).
jainism.tie_back: The heroine is caught between those very two, the pull to sulk and the pull to embrace, which Jainism counsels cutting away together.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; names the same two pulls (love and aversion) but treats them as bonds to cut, not as the play of married love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus stands before her at last, Penelope sits silent, pondering whether to question her husband from a distance or to go to him and kiss his head and hands, and Telemachus scolds her for her hardness of heart.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer gives Penelope a long moment of doubt between reserve and embrace before she yields.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s dilemma almost exactly: hold back or embrace, or somehow both.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene; a very close parallel on a wife torn between reserve and embrace at her husband’s return, though Penelope’s reserve is caution rather than a sulk.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza calls it vacillation of mind when the same thing is at once the cause of both joy and sorrow, so that we love and hate it at once.
philosophy.explanation: Spinoza explains how one object can stir opposite feelings at the same moment.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s undecided ‘shall I sulk or embrace?’ is exactly such a vacillation toward one beloved person.
philosophy.source: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics III, Proposition 17 and Scholium (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a standard passage; good conceptual fit for mixed feelings, though the Kural’s pique is playful rather than true hatred.

kurals.tamil:
வினைகலந்து வென்றீக வேந்தன் மனைகலந்து
மாலை அயர்கம் விருந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Vinaikalandhu vendreeka vaendhan manaikalandhu
maalai ayarkam virundhu.
kurals.meaning: Let the king press on with the campaign and win; then I will go home to my wife and we will feast together this evening.
kurals.elementary: Now the husband speaks. He is far away helping the king in a big contest. He thinks: “Let us finish this job and win, and then I can rush home and have a happy dinner with my wife tonight.” He misses her just as much as she misses him.
kurals.university: Here the speaker changes: it is the husband, serving with the king (vēntaṉ) on campaign, who voices his own vitumpal, which is why the chapter is ‘mutual’. Viṉai kalantu veṉṟīka, ‘may [the king] engage in the task and win’, is followed by maṉai kalantu, ‘joining my home (wife)’, and mālai ayarkam viruntu, ‘we shall hold a feast in the evening’. The parallel kalantu…kalantu sets the king’s battle beside the husband’s reunion. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read the hero’s eagerness for victory as eagerness to be home; Puliyur Kesikan specifies ‘with her in the evening’. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: During the monsoon at Kishkindha, Rama, separated from Sita, laments that the rains delay the campaign to recover her, and longs for the season to end so that he can march and win her back.
hinduism.explanation: Valmiki shows a hero whose impatience for the campaign is really impatience to be reunited with his wife.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s husband, Rama wants the fighting done because his heart is with his wife.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, Rama’s lament in the rains (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; partial fit, since Rama must first fight to reach Sita, whereas the Kural’s husband waits for the king’s war to end.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of the life of thy vanity, which he hath given thee under the sun… for that is thy portion in this life, and in thy labour which thou takest under the sun.”
christianity.explanation: The Preacher names joy with one’s beloved wife as the true portion of life amid all labour.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s husband feels the same: the campaign is labour, and the evening with his wife is his real reward.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV; ellipsis marks an omitted phrase); a strong match on joy with one’s wife as the end of labour.

islam.quote_or_event: When Abdullah ibn Amr fasted every day and prayed all night, the Prophet told him not to, saying that his body, his eyes and his wife each have a right over him.
islam.explanation: The Prophet restrains even devout effort that crowds out a man’s duty of companionship to his wife.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s husband feels the same claim: his wife’s right draws him home once the task is done.
islam._accuracy_note: Hadith text checked on sunnah.com and given as paraphrase; good match on a wife’s claim balancing a man’s outward duties, though the duty in question is worship, not war.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When a man taketh a new wife, he shall not go out in the host, neither shall he be charged with any business; he shall be free for his house one year, and shall cheer his wife whom he hath taken.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah exempts a newly married man from war so that he can make his wife happy.
judaism.tie_back: Torah law gives priority to exactly what the Kural’s husband longs for: leaving the campaign to be with his wife.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a strong match on war yielding to a husband’s duty of joy to his wife.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When, after a long absence, a man safely returns from afar, his relatives, friends and well-wishers welcome him home on arrival.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses a traveller’s homecoming as a picture of joyful welcome.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the homecoming the Kural’s husband is already imagining: the work done, a welcome and a feast at home.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; good image match, though the verse is a simile for good deeds welcoming one in the next life.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Give up your wealth and your wife; you have entered the state of the houseless; do not, as it were, return to your vomit; Gautama, &c.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira tells a monk not to look back toward the household and wife he has left.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband longs to hurry home to his wife; Jain teaching for the renouncer points the other way, though it does not forbid this to the householder.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a candid contrast addressed to monks, not a parallel; no closer Jain source on a husband’s longing was found.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: On Calypso’s island, Odysseus sits on the shore day after day weeping, longing for his homecoming and his wife, though a goddess offers him immortality to stay.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer’s hero values the return to his home and wife above everything else on offer.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s husband shares this pull: whatever the task, his heart is set on the evening at home with his wife.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous scene; strong match on a husband longing for home, though Odysseus is held captive rather than serving a king.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle writes that we are busy in order to have leisure, and make war in order to live in peace.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, work and war are not ends in themselves but are for the sake of the life lived afterward.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s husband sees the king’s war the same way: it is for the sake of the evening feast at home.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10.7 (tr. W.D. Ross; paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known sentence; a strong structural match, though Aristotle’s ‘leisure’ points toward contemplation rather than domestic love.

kurals.tamil:
ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல் செல்லும்சேண் சென்றார்
வருநாள்வைத்து ஏங்கு பவர்க்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Orunaal ezhunaalpoal sellumsaen sendraar
varunaal-vaiththu aengu pavarkku.
kurals.meaning: For those who pine with their minds set on the day their faraway beloved will return, a single day drags by like seven.
kurals.elementary: Do you remember waiting for your birthday or a holiday? The last few days feel sooo long! The verse says that when you are waiting for someone you love to come home, one day can feel as long as a whole week.
kurals.university: A general maxim (note the plural ēṅkupavarkku, ‘for those who pine’) caps the chapter’s experience: oru nāḷ eḻu nāḷ pōl cellum, ‘one day passes like seven’, for those who have fixed in mind (vaittu) the day (varu nāḷ) of return of one who has gone far (cēṇ ceṉṟār). Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the seven; Solomon Pappaiah generalises to ‘many days’; Kalaignar heightens it to ‘each day like an age (yugam)’. The commentary tradition associated with Parimelazhagar takes it as spoken by the heroine of herself, generalised into a truth. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “When You go off to the forest during the day, a tiny fraction of a second becomes like a millennium for us because we cannot see You.”
hinduism.explanation: The gopis tell Krishna that every moment without the sight of him stretches into an age.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim, magnified: for the one who waits, a day is seven days, or a moment a millennium.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 10.31.15 (tr. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io (first sentence of the translation); a near one-to-one match on time stretched by separation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My soul waiteth for the Lord more than they that watch for the morning: I say, more than they that watch for the morning.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist compares his waiting to night watchmen longing for the dawn, when every hour drags.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s waiter, the watchman knows how slowly time passes when you are waiting for an arrival.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); good fit on the long hours of waiting, though it does not state the time distortion directly.

islam.quote_or_event: “And they urge you to hasten the punishment. But Allah will never fail in His promise. And indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of those which you count.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an reminds the impatient that time is measured differently with God than by human counting.
islam.tie_back: The Kural also says that a day is not always a day: for the yearning heart, it stretches far beyond its count.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via api.alquran.cloud (en.sahih); next-best match: it shares the idea of one day equalling many, but the point is divine time, not a lover’s impatience.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her.”
judaism.explanation: Jacob’s love for Rachel makes seven years of labour feel like a few days.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts say love bends time by the number seven; for Jacob, with his goal in sight, years shrink, while for the Kural’s waiting lover a day swells into seven.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); a precise mirror image of the Kural (love shortening rather than lengthening time).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Long is the night to the sleepless; long is the league to the weary. Long is worldly existence to fools who know not the Sublime Truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that time and distance stretch for those who are suffering.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s waiting lover lives the first line: her nights and days are long because she is restless with longing.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a close match on subjective time lengthened by suffering, though the verse’s point is about ignorance of the Dhamma.

jainism.quote_or_event: “As the fallow leaf of the tree falls to the ground, when its days are gone, even so the life of men (will come to its close); Gautama, be careful all the while!”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira reminds Gautama that human life is short and urges him not to waste a single moment.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s lover feels each day as long; Jain teaching asks one to feel each moment as precious, a contrasting lesson about the weight of time.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; next-best match: it concerns the value of time, but not the stretching of time in longing.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Theocritus opens an idyll of welcome to a returning beloved by saying that those who long grow old in a single day.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek pastoral poetry states that longing makes one day as heavy as years.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is nearly the Kural’s own maxim: for the one who waits, a day is far longer than a day.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known line; a near one-to-one match, though from Hellenistic poetry rather than myth proper.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Bergson observes that if he wants a glass of sugar-water he must wait until the sugar melts, and that this time of waiting is not a mathematical quantity but coincides with his impatience, a portion of his own lived duration.
philosophy.explanation: Bergson distinguishes clock time from lived time, which stretches with impatience.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural says the same: by the clock it is one day, but in the waiting heart it is seven.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous example; a strong conceptual match on lived time stretched by impatience, though not about love.

kurals.tamil:
பெறின்என்னாம் பெற்றக்கால் என்னாம் உறினென்னாம்
உள்ளம் உடைந்துக்கக் கால்.
kurals.transliteration:
Perin-ennaam petrakkaal ennaam urinennaam
ullam udaindhukkak kaal.
kurals.meaning: If her heart breaks and she perishes from the grief of waiting, what use will it be that she gets me back, has me back, or even holds me again?
kurals.elementary: The husband worries: “If I stay away too long, she might become so sad that her heart breaks. Then what good would it be to come home? I must hurry back while there is still time.” It is like a promise that is only worth something if you keep it in time.
kurals.university: Most commentators, following the tradition associated with Parimelazhagar, give this closing couplet to the husband, who fears for his wife: Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘if her heart breaks… what use is it that she gets me?’, and Pope translates ‘If she heart-broken lie, with all her life poured forth’. The triple question peṟiṉ eṉ ām / peṟṟakkāl eṉ ām / uṟiṉ eṉ ām moves from ‘should she obtain [me]’ to ‘having obtained’ to ‘having embraced’, and uḷḷam uṭaintu ukkakkāl means ‘when the heart has broken and spilled away’, a euphemism for dying of grief. Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the first person plural (நம்மை) and Kalaignar a neutral ‘each other’, so the speaker is not unanimous, but the sense of urgency is shared. Text agrees on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Queen Indumati dies suddenly, King Aja laments that without her his kingdom, his pleasures and his very life have lost their meaning, and he lives on only for his son’s sake.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa shows that every good a husband possesses becomes empty once the beloved wife is gone.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the fear behind the Kural: if she dies of grief, no reunion, victory or embrace will be worth anything.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Raghuvamsha, canto 8, Aja’s lament for Indumati (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous lament; good match on life emptied by a wife’s death, though Indumati’s death is not caused by separation.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus asks what any gain is worth if the one thing that matters is lost.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s husband asks the same kind of question: what use is any homecoming if she is lost?
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bible-api.com (KJV); shares the rhetorical ‘what profit’ structure, but its subject is the soul, not a spouse.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s romance, Majnun, kept apart from Layla all his life, learns of her death and goes to her grave, where he dies; their union comes only in death.
islam.explanation: The great Persian love story shows separation lasting until it is too late for any earthly reunion.
islam.tie_back: This is the outcome the Kural’s husband dreads: a heart broken by separation, after which meeting means nothing.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a classical Persian romance (Islamic literary culture, not scripture); good match on love undone by prolonged separation.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity; but a broken spirit who can bear?”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says the spirit can carry bodily illness, but nothing can carry a broken spirit.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s husband fears precisely a broken spirit (uḷḷam uṭaintu) that nothing afterward could mend.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on mechon-mamre.org (JPS 1917); close on the gravity of a broken heart, without the Kural’s urgency to return in time.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Therefore hold nothing dear, for separation from the dear is painful. There are no bonds for those who have nothing beloved or unloved.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that separation from loved ones is inherently painful and counsels non-attachment.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s couple know that pain of separation all too well; the husband’s answer is to hurry home, the Buddha’s is to loosen the bond.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it names the same pain of separation but prescribes the opposite remedy.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.”
jainism.explanation: Forsaken by Arishtanemi, Rajimati feels that her life as it was has lost its worth, and turns to renunciation.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati is the heart-broken wife the Kural’s husband fears to leave behind, though in Jainism her grief opens onto a new path.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a genuine picture of a forsaken woman’s despair, but the story resolves in renunciation rather than reunion.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Theseus, sailing home victorious from Crete, forgets to raise the white sail; his father Aegeus, watching from the cliff and seeing the black sail, throws himself into the sea, so that Theseus’ triumphant return comes too late.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth shows a victory made empty because the one waiting at home did not survive the wait.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s warning in story form: if the one at home is lost to grief, the return and the victory are worth nothing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth; a strong match on a return made worthless by the waiting one’s death, though the bond is father and son.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca urges his friend to hold every hour fast, since everything else belongs to others and time alone is truly ours, and once lost it cannot be recovered.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca treats time as the one irreplaceable possession, which delay squanders.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s husband sees the same danger: delay could cost what no later return can restore.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 1 (tr. R.M. Gummere; paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous letter; next-best match on the urgency of time, though Seneca is not speaking of love.
